messages.subject: a mixture-model expression in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I was corresponding with someone who was trying to use Stan for models with discrete parameters, using the mixture model formulation as explained in the manual.  He felt that the log-probability specification was hard for users in his subfield to understand.  This made me think, maybe we could add a new distribution called finite_mixture or something like that, where the arguments are the probabilities and the mixture distributions. I’m not quite sure how this would be done—to do it in sufficient generality to be useful might end up being even more complicated to use—but I just wanted to throw this idea out there.
A

messages.subject: WAIC in Stan
messages.body_plain:
On Mar 1, 2014, at 5:09 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> I agree that we should just implement the calculation in Stan C++ so that Waic is not tied to R.

This is going to be tricky for reasons I pointed out
that it's going to need cross-chain and cross-draw information,
so it can't go in the Stan language directly.

But I'd still like to have a reference implementation.

Daniel --- any thoughts on how to share bin/print-like functionality
across CmdStan, RStan and PyStan?  Do we need an interface for
chains, etc., like the extract() function in R?

> Also, one thing I’d like, which I think should be very easy in Stan C++, is to be able to calculate WAIC for any sort of object called log_lik.  That is, log_lik could be a scalar, a vector, an array, a matrix, a vector of arrays, an array of vectors, whatever, and what Stan would do is compute the sums and variances in the WAIC calculation by using the individual components of log_lik.  (For example, if log_lik is a 3x4x5 array, WAIC would be calculated using the 24 elements of the array.)

I think that's 60 elements, and we already have a feature request
for a flatten() function:  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/575

>
> If I want the R code to do this, I’ll need to add some code between the first and second lines of the current waic() function to convert the R object log_lik into a vector.
>
> Also I think that at the same time that we add log_lik to Stan C++, we should also allow the user to pass a whitelist of variables to save or a blacklist of variables to not save.  In particular, I’m thinking that we might but log_lik in the blacklist by default, so that the user will only get it if he or she puts it in the whitelist.  I say this because I can imagine a world in which it becomes standard to calculate WAIC for models, and if there’s a big dataset with thousands or millions of data points, we don’t want to be spewing all this out.

These would be two separate features, but they could go in at the same
time.

So you're saying blacklist and whitelist, but the whitelist takes precedence?
That's pretty ugly and doesn't admit very easy error checking.

I take it this is all "for the future" or for someone else to do as a project,
not something I should start working on right away?

- Bob

messages.subject: prob propto 1/sigma
messages.body_plain:
>From Andrew:

> ... is there a way we can include that prior p(sigma) proportional to 1/sigma more transparently, instead of increment_log_prob?  Or maybe increment_log_prob is the clearest approach.

I assume

  increment_log_prob(log(1/sigma));

is not what you meant :-)

It's not a proper density is it?  Should we add improper densities?
We could also add an improper:

  y ~ flat();

If so, you can make a feature request on GitHub, and preferably
again let us know about priority?  Or I can do it if you think we
should.

You can almost get there with a Pareto with very small
shape and lower bound, as in:

  sigma ~ pareto(1e-30, 1e-30);

which will make sigma proportional to (1/y)^(1 + 1e-30), and the
1 + 1e-30 will underflow to 1.    But it also requires that pesky
lower bound.

- Bob

gives the 1/sigma prior.  Remember, 1/sigma implies uniform for log(sigma).

messages.subject: Re: [RFC] Convergence test
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, February 24, 2014 5:54:33 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Alternatively, one could thin the chains so that approximate independence of retained draws is a reasonable assumption and obtain the p-value for a test of the null hypothesis that all the chains have the same distribution. To do this, we can use the distance correlation concept of Székely, Rizzo, and Bakirov (2007)
>
> https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdfview_1/euclid.aos/1201012979
>
> which has the property that two possibly multivariate random variables A and B are independent iff the distance correlation between them is zero. We can estimate the distance correlation at time t by rowwise stacking the m draws at time t into the matrix A and rowwise stacking the m draws at time t - j into the matrix B for some j > 0 lags (the columns of both A and B are the posterior parameters). There is a bias-corrected version of the distance correlation estimator in the bcdcor() function in the energy package for R. We can then plot nonparametric curves of these distance correlations over time by j to see what lag length renders the draws essentially independent. This particular graph is fairly easy to interpret, such as in the case of the leuk model from the BUGS examples:

I made the plot below to compare the posterior dependence of MH, NUTS, and Gibbs. Again, the estimated dependence at a particular iteration is consistent as the number of chains increases.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-9L5Vv5Sqb6E/UxO91GBvPkI/AAAAAAAAAOE/-lGN9jXvhYY/s1600/dependence.png>
The example is low birthweight as a function of age, race, and smoking from MCMCpack. MCMClogit is a MH sampler with scaled Cauchy priors on the coefficients that jumps from a multivariate normal with covariance matrix proportional to the estimated variance-covariance matrix of the MLE estimates. It has about a 25% acceptance rate. The same model in Stan with an 80% targeted acceptance rate has much less dependence. Stan is almost as good as the MCMCprobit implementation, which has a noninformative multivariate normal prior on the coefficients and updates them in one batch from their full-conditional distribution given the data-augmented latent variable.

Whether you go on to say that the Stan draws are essentially independent after three or four lags and then test the null hypothesis of convergence to the same distribution is another question (although you would fail to reject in this case). I still don't see why whether or not the covariances among thinned MCMC draws converge to anything matters if the test only requires the existence of first moments.

Ben

messages.subject: Final call for feedback on proposal for functions
messages.subject_clean: Final call for feedback on proposal for functions
messages.body_plain:
I revised the proposal w.r.t. everyone's suggestions and removed
alternatives that are now off the table.   Some other changes:

* allow constrained types in declarations and return that get
  checked on input and output

* changed subroutines to "submodels", removed "void" altogether
  and put them in their own block to clarify

* added a proposal for functions ending in "_rng" to have access
  to the PRNG base in order to allow meaningful generated quantities
  functions

* added some other suggestions (solvers for roots, non-constant args,
  Boost tuples [better idea than structs!]) and tried to clearly mark
  things I won't implement in the first pass as FUTURE

Let me know if there are any more comments, because I'd like to
start building this as soon as the parser fixes get merged.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: C++11 dependencies?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks very much for all the clarifications.

I'm happy deprecating support of llvm-g++-4.2.  I think Apple's
pretty much doing that anyway.

That'd be awesome if we could replace Boost's promote_args with auto.
I'd imagine we could do it for internal variables that are declared
and defined in one go, but the compiler would have to be very smart
to figure out function return types, wouldn't it?  For instance, if
we do something like this:

  return x > 0 : var(x) : 0;

how can it figure out the return is var?

- Bob

> On Monday, March 3, 2014 11:55:57 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I thought Rcpp compiled (or at least used to) under C++11?
>
> I think it does for everything except llvm-g++-4.2 on Mac.
>
> Does it even matter for the level at which they're interfacing?
>
> As long as CRAN sticks with its plan to have an option to build the binary Mac package with clang++, then probably not for most packages that depend on it. I haven't checked as to whether there would be any problems linking with a C++11 version of Rcpp if RStan doesn't specify -std=c++11.
>
> Thanks for the tips on Windows and Mac.
>
> We absolutely need to keep compatibility with all platforms (Windows,
> Mac, Linux), and both RStan and PyStan.
>
> If we could get to the point where we say llvm-g++-4.2 isn't supported for RStan anymore, then we could at least use auto and decltype, which would be a lot cleaner than all the boost::promote_args<> stuff. I'm not sure if the mingw that comes with Rtools supports much more C++11 than that.

That's whack. No idea why it's trying to allocate so many bytes here.
The error makes it look like it's trying to swap:

> FATAL: MemorySanitizer can not mmap the shadow memory.

Any idea what PIE or -pie are?

> FATAL: Make sure to compile with -fPIE and to link with -pie.
> FATAL: Disabling ASLR is known to cause this error.

ASLR?  That looks like "address space layout randomization".  Does
that mean the test is just jumping up where it tries to do the allocation
each time?  That doesn't seem realistic, but would cause the fail.

> FATAL: If running under GDB, try 'set disable-randomization off'.

Is that supposed to un-disable ASLR?  Too many negations!

But it is jumped way up in memory:

>
>         0xffffffffff600000-0xffffffffff601000   [vsyscall]
> ==1550==End of process memory map.
> make: *** [test/unit/memory/stack_alloc_speed] Error 77

Thanks for trying!

>

>
> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ cat src/test/unit/memory/stack_alloc_speed_test.cpp
> #include <stan/memory/stack_alloc.hpp>

>
> TEST(stack_alloc, speed_of_allocator) {
>   stan::memory::stack_alloc allocator;
>   for (size_t m = 0; m < 10000; m++) {
>     for (size_t n = 1; n <= 100000; ++n) {
>       allocator.alloc(n);
>     }
>     allocator.recover_all();
>   }
> }

I think that's more illuminating because chaning that to 10K, it's 10K * 10K, so
it should just use 100MB.  Whereas with 100K * 10K, it's using 1GB.  Still, I
wouldn't think that'd balk.

I don't see why recover_all doesn't reset back to the beginning.  Here's
the code:

      inline void recover_all() {
        cur_block_ = 0;
        next_loc_ = blocks_[0];
        cur_block_end_ = next_loc_ + sizes_[0];
      }

These ever-shifting C++ compilers are really frustrating.    I take it you
did this in earlier compilers without a problem?

Here's the sanitizer code that's throwing the error:

  https://llvm.org/svn/llvm-project/compiler-rt/trunk/lib/msan/msan_allocator.cc

But I'm not going to worry about it if only the sanitizer is causing
problems.  From looking at the code, it looks like it never deallocs (see
MSanDeallocate function). It's own doc:

http://clang.llvm.org/docs/MemorySanitizer.html

says it's an experimental tool.

Also, we don't want to check that all of our allocated memory is
clean --- we intentionally allocate memory that we don't ever fill
because we have sizes that overrun boundaries of blocks so have to
go in the next block.  Could this be the source of the problem?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
_rng() will only be callable from generated quantities, matching
our current restrictions on the PRNGs.

We could allow RNG in transformed data, but the problem we
discussed with that before (or maybe I just discussed with
myself before we had a bigger team) was that there's no way to
get the transformed data back out.

We could probably generalize the commands somehow to allow transformed
data to have access.  We'd have to push the seed through to the
model constructor, as right now it's only being passed in
later.

But that's an independent issue.  The "_rng" functions will follow
the use of the other PRNGs.

I really don't like these naming conventions, by the way.  Right
now, the compiler looks to see if a function ends in "_rng" and if
so, implicitly passes the PRNG base function to it.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] prob propto 1/sigma
messages.body_plain:
The parameters are all uniform by default on their
constrained values.

So if you declare:

   real<lower=0> sigma;

then sigma is uniform on (0,inf).

What happens under the hood is that there is an unconstrained
parameter sigma_raw with support on (-inf,inf), and then
sigma is defined by the inverse-log transform:

  sigma <- exp(sigma_raw);

and the total log probability is incremented by the log Jacobian,
here log(abs(exp'(sigma_raw))) = sigma_raw, so that the effect is

  lp__ <- lp__ + sigma_raw;

The unconstrained representantations and Jacobians are all
detailed in a chapter near the end of the manual.

So when Andrew takes sigma propto 1/sigma, the effect is:

  lp__ <- lp__ + log(1/sigma);

which reduces to

  lp__ <- lp__ - sigma;

so it cancels the Jacobian and leaves the transform of
sigma uniform, i.e., log(sigma) propto constant.

And before anyone asks, let me say that Stan isn't smart
enough to avoid adding sigma and subtracting sigma --- it
just does both operations and calculates gradients with respect
to both and it all cancels arithmetically, not symbolically.

- Bob

Ah, I figured it out. Not a bug.

I couple days ago I configured that tab to limit the memory of a process to 2GB when I was trying to investigate that memory leak that I emailed you about. Then I forgot I was using that same tab when I was trying to do the unit tests.

That said, we need to keep all individual tests below 2GB (at least with clang++) because the most basic tier of availability on the Columbia cluster is limited to 2GB per process. There are hundreds of cores available for that purpose and we can basically do 1 core per unit test. If you need more memory, you have to wait for one of the much fewer number of big memory slots to become available.

Ben

whether to deal with functions that want to manipulate the log probability
accumulator.

messages.subject: vectorizing lower/upper bounds for constrained variables
messages.subject_clean: vectorizing lower/upper bounds for constrained variables
messages.body_plain:
On Mar 4, 2014, at 8:39 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> The limitation that lower and upper bounds can only be scalars is pretty limiting in my opinion.
>

This is a separate issue from the function language, so I dropped
it in a new thread.

I agree that it's limiting.

It's a bit tricky to extend the language, but it'd be a great
project.

The main issue is how to test that the lower/upper bounds conform
to the dimensions of the variable.

Case 1.

  real<lower=L,upper=U> a[N];

If L and U are either scalars or 1D arrays of size N,
it's easy.  Should we also allow row vectors or column vectors?

Case 2.

  real<lower=L,upper=U> b[M,N];

Here I think we'd want L and U to be 2D arrays (maybe matrices,
arrays of vectors, etc.?)

Case 3.

  vector<lower=L,upper=U>[N] x;

Again, this is easy if L or U are scalars or 1D vectors of size
N (or arrays?  or row vectors?).

Case 4.

  vector<lower=L,upper=U>[N] x[M];

Here I think it makes sense to take L to be scalars or 1D
vectors (arrays/row vectors) of size N.  But should we also
allow matrices (arrays) of size M x N?  Or mixtures of vectors
and matrices?

- Bob

We have the same sort of issue with the never-implemented syntax

matrix ~ distribution(vector, scalar);

as in

Y ~ normal(mu_vec, sigma);

so whatever we decide is supported for that, we might as do the same thing the bounds on declared parameters.

I think my position was "all pieces must match each other exactly (in type and size), except that a scalar matches with anything". So, the above would actually be illegal unless the user broadcasted mu_vec into a matrix with the same dimensions as Y.

Ben

messages.subject: CmdStan is now out of Stan
messages.subject_clean: CmdStan is now out of Stan
messages.body_plain:
I've posted the first set of instructions here:
https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/wiki/Getting-Started-with-CmdStan

Please feel free to edit or comment where it's not clear or is inaccurate.

Anyone that used Stan as CmdStan, you should go and clone CmdStan. Stan is now going to be a submodule and although it's a little tricky, it's not really that bad.

The nice thing is that you can go and use the Stan submodule like you would the current repository. That means you can branch, commit, and push from the Stan submodule and it'll have the same effect as if it were the actual repository.

The model targets are the same as before:
- make build: will build bin/print and bin/stanc
- make bin/print or make bin/stanc: that will build the binaries independently
- make foo/bar: that will build the Stan model in foo/bar.stan. It will leave foo/bar.cpp as an artifact.
- make foo/bar.cpp: that will generate the C++, but not compile it.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: updating Boost and Eigen
messages.body_plain:
Might be offtopic, but: Supporting a range of Boost and Eigen versions
rather than just the latest is valuable, because most
OSes/distributions do not always package the latest-and-greatest.
This probably means not packaging Boost/Eigen/GTest with Stan directly
where possible, and using something like Vagrant or Docker to create
CI/build slaves that build/test in each OS/distribution, then simply
stating Boost, Eigen, etc. as dependencies and checking for them in
the configure/make step.

Barring that, more fodder for why following latest stable seems like a
good idea: it's hard to justify "you have to use specific version X of
this dependency and specific version Y of that dependency" to users if
those versions aren't the latest version when an inevitable
incompatibility/interface change happens.

That said, I understand the Eigen dependency is indivisible, but for
Boost if you want to reduce overhead, it is possible to just
use/package the libraries of boost that stan uses specifically rather
than all of boost. [1][2][3]

[1]   https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/wiki/ModBigPicture
[2] https://github.com/boostorg/boost
[3]   https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/wiki/CMakeModularizationStatus

reduce size.  But Boost likes to include other packages, so it's

in new pieces.

of Boost or Eigen.   The main problem with supporting multiple versions is
that we don't have the testing compute power or person power to
run all the combinatorics.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] use JSON as data input file format
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] use JSON as data input file format
messages.body_plain:
Awesome! Questions / comments:
- I'm good with scalars and one dimensional data types. That's the Stan types: vector, row vector, and 1-d real array (e.g. real x[2])
- For 2-d data types,
  * `matrix[2,3] b` is stored as row major and as a JSON arrays. That's fine by me.
  * `real b[2,3]` is also stored as row major and as a JSON array. That makes sense. That's two JSON arrays of length 3 inside a JSON array. This looks identical to matrix[2,3].
  * `vector[3] b[2]` looks like there's a JSON array of length 2 made up of JSON arrays of length 3. I think that makes sense. So each internal array lines up with the actual Stan type. This also looks identical to matrix[2,3].
  * `row_vector[2] b[3]` -- I don't think this makes sense as specified. It looks like "b: [ [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6] ]" and looks identical to matrix[2,3]. I think it should be specified as 3 JSON arrays of JSON arrays of length 2. So something like: "b: [ [1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6] ]". I think if we were to follow this pattern, we can extend this to multiple dimensions.
- Arbitrary dimensions? So what do we do about `matrix[2,3] c[4]` or `vector[4] c[2,3]`? For the first, I would expect there to be a JSON array of length 4 made up of 2x3 matrices. For the second, I would expect there to be a JSON array of length 2 which has a JSON array of length 3 made up of what we read in as a vector.

Thoughts?

Daniel

There are a couple typos that I've taken care of. Just for reference, the ones I've found:

Variable declarations:
- "1-dimensional vector: real a[5]; (all vectors are vectors of reals)." -- changed to "vector[5] a;"
- "array of row vetor: row_vector[2] b[3];" -- changed to "vetor"

Stan variable definitions as JSON name : value pairs
- fixed duplicate array of row vectors
- "vetor" -> "vector"

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] use JSON as data input file format
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] use JSON as data input file format
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the comments!

>
>   * `real b[2,3]` is also stored as row major and as a JSON array. That makes sense. That's two JSON arrays of length 3 inside a JSON array. This looks identical to matrix[2,3].

yes - in JSON notation a matrix and 2D array look the same.  the Stan I/O must match variable declarations to definitions to enforce the semantics.

>   * `vector[3] b[2]` looks like there's a JSON array of length 2 made up of JSON arrays of length 3. I think that makes sense. So each internal array lines up with the actual Stan type. This also looks identical to matrix[2,3].

yes.

>   * `row_vector[2] b[3]` -- I don't think this makes sense as specified. It looks like "b: [ [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6] ]" and looks identical to matrix[2,3]. I think it should be specified as 3 JSON arrays of JSON arrays of length 2. So something like: "b: [ [1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6] ]". I think if we were to follow this pattern, we can extend this to multiple dimensions.

yes, you're correct - this is what it should be and I've edited the wiki page accordingly.

> - Arbitrary dimensions? So what do we do about `matrix[2,3] c[4]` or `vector[4] c[2,3]`? For the first, I would expect there to be a JSON array of length 4 made up of 2x3 matrices. For the second, I would expect there to be a JSON array of length 2 which has a JSON array of length 3 made up of what we read in as a vector.

yes, exactly.  I've added these to the wiki page as well.

> There are a couple typos that I've taken care of. Just for reference, the ones I've found:

many thanks!

Mitzi

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: updating Boost and Eigen
messages.body_plain:
I'd like to echo this point. If we ever want to get into the Debian/Ubuntu or
Redhat/Centos ecosystem (which would be great since it would elimiate the
initial compile of libstan.a) it would be useful/mandatory to be able to compile
against the distribution's version of Boost and Eigen.

For example, the new Ubuntu 14.04 (due in April and a "long term support"
version) will have boost 1.54.0 and Eigen 3.2.0 available.

Best,

-a

On 03/05, Ido Rosen wrote:
> Might be offtopic, but: Supporting a range of Boost and Eigen versions
> rather than just the latest is valuable, because most
> OSes/distributions do not always package the latest-and-greatest.
> This probably means not packaging Boost/Eigen/GTest with Stan directly
> where possible, and using something like Vagrant or Docker to create
> CI/build slaves that build/test in each OS/distribution, then simply
> stating Boost, Eigen, etc. as dependencies and checking for them in
> the configure/make step.
>
> Barring that, more fodder for why following latest stable seems like a
> good idea: it's hard to justify "you have to use specific version X of
> this dependency and specific version Y of that dependency" to users if
> those versions aren't the latest version when an inevitable
> incompatibility/interface change happens.
>
> That said, I understand the Eigen dependency is indivisible, but for
> Boost if you want to reduce overhead, it is possible to just
> use/package the libraries of boost that stan uses specifically rather
> than all of boost. [1][2][3]
>
> [1]   https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/wiki/ModBigPicture
> [2] https://github.com/boostorg/boost
> [3]   https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/wiki/CMakeModularizationStatus
>
>
> On Wed, Mar 5, 2014 at 12:02 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > On Mar 5, 2014, at 5:57 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> Eigen changes more on a relative basis than Boost because it is a younger project, but I don't see anything here
> >>
> >> http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/index.php?title=ChangeLog#Eigen_3.2.1
> >>
> >> that is super-relevant to Stan.
> >
> > Mainly bug fixes and speed improvements.
> >
> >> Boost 1.55 apparently doesn't (entirely?) work with Visual Studio 2013 which some guy on stan-users recently got to work
> >>
> >> http://www.boost.org/users/history/version_1_55_0.html
> >>
> >> but it is harder to keep track of the changelog of Boost and know whether there is something of benefit to those that don't do Visual Studio.
> >
> > It's not critical that we update, either.  It just seems easier
> > to me to keep updating as we go than do it all in one big lump
> > later.  Maybe that's not the case.
> >
> > - Bob

I think CRAN is a more relevant target than Linux distributions because there are many more problems installing from source on Mac / Windows than there are Linux users of Stan. But if we were to satisfy CRAN, then satisfying Linux distributions would be easier if not automatic.

At the moment, RcppEigen is at 0.3.2.1.x, which is the version we are considering upgrading to. In general, the greater problem with RcppEigen is that it might get upgraded before Stan is ready to do so, but Eigen is hyper-concerned with backward compatibility.

More problematic, BH is at 1.51, which does not include odeint and a couple other things. I imagine we could request that BH go to 1.54, but I haven't done so yet because I haven't managed to get consensus that having RStan on CRAN would be worthwhile. I suspect that Dirk either uses 1.51 at his day job or is waiting until Debian Testing transitions to a more recent Boost (96% there to 1.54 according to https://release.debian.org/transitions/ but this may actually turn into Boost 1.55).

The point I keep trying to emphasize is that if we were to get RStan onto CRAN, then we would have less of a maintenance burden overall
Binary installs are easier so more people install it and thus field-test it on hardware that we don't have
We would be covered by CRAN policies so uploads of Rcpp (or RcppEigen or BH) that break RStan builds or unit-tests aren't allowed
Easier for R developers who are depending on RStan

So, if that means that we have to maintain 1+ versions, either by putting patched versions of Boost or Eigen headers into RStan earlier on the PATH or even different versions of the libraries for CmdStan, I think it would be worth it.

Ben

On Saturday, March 8, 2014 5:36:16 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Can we somehow guarantee that if Rcpp works, then RStan will work?

Beyond RStan's unit tests, no. But there is the CRAN principle (that Dirk follows as maintainer of Rcpp, BH, and RcppEigen) that if a new version of a dependency package causes RStan's unit tests to fail, then it is supposed to get sorted out before the new dependency package goes onto CRAN.

> Installing Rcpp has been problematic for some users, despite its
> being on CRAN, but the question is really whether it will assume
> enough of a C++ toolchain for us?  Or are there still make issues
> that can bite us or version issues with C++ compilers?

Installing Rcpp has been a problem, but we really should just refer those problems to the Rcpp list. There is reason to think that things will be better with the next version of R in April, which will have an environmental variable to compile under the C++11 standard (meaning with clang++ instead of llvm-g++-4.2 for Macs). So, we could probably abandon llvm-g++-4.2 at that point. RStan users would still have to have a toolchain to compile their models, but we could think about splitting RStan into two parts so that users would be able to run models that someone else compiled (e.g. CRAN for rstanarm).

> As to testing (vs. Rcpp, RcppEigen, Boost tools, etc.), are we going to
> be able to compile models and test running them and extracting results part
> of our tests?  I thought there were serious limitations on the time CRAN will
> allow.  In fact, I thought the compile time for bin/stanc was a dealbreaker
> in and of itself for getting RStan on CRAN.

Not the compile time, the "minimum necessary size on disk". We were deemed not minimal due to bundling a giant chunk of Boost that could have been a system requirement (or a dependency on a future BH package). There is a limit of 5 minutes of wall time for testing / vignettes but we could do a couple of simple models.

> Would CRAN distribution mean our binary will go out with -O2 compilation
> through some version of g++?  If so, I'd like to test the performance hit
> (if any).   Or can we specify our own optimization level?  I'm not
> very good at remembering all the dependencies (hence my obsession with
> reducing their number), but don't we have optimization-level dependencies
> with Windows?

The package flags trump the R flags (and are trumped by the user's flags, but there is no user on CRAN). But I think stanc compiles under Windows with -O2 as long as there is no -g.

Ben

> On Mar 10, 2014, at 2:50 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
>> Do/should we have a "circular" datatype in Stan?  That is, it's defined on a circle
>> rather than the line, so that HMC will go spinning around?
>
> I think we already addressed this one and it's tricky because it
> introduces discontinuity.  But I'm posting on stan-dev to let

It’s much, much harder than it looks — because the topology of a circle S^{1} is different from
R^{1} there is no smooth map from one to the other.  A naive sine/cosine transform, for example,
leads to an infinite sum.  This is the fundamental reason why circular statistics are such a fricken
mess.

In practice, however, there is a trick.  If we sample n + 1 variables and the divide by the sum of
their squares then we get an unidentified sphere, S^{n}.  If we then add a gaussian prior to each
of the n + 1 variables we get reasonable identifiability without affecting the sampling.  It’s a dirty
trick that would require modifying the log posterior, but it would work for the most part.

messages.subject: example of flaky chain
messages.body_plain:
Should we create a separate repo for problematic model/data + sampling
configs?

For the model I posted on Andrew's blog (data and model attached),
I was finding that with different seeds, one of the four chains would
sometimes fail.

With this call:

./pk_iv_oral sample id=19 random seed=1 data file=data.R

I get a traceplot for c0 where a chain temporarily jumps to a value
like 1e16, whereas other chains give it a posterior mean of around 9.
This, of course, drives n_eff to roughly 0 and tanks the R-hat stat.

The treedepth mean goes from 4 to 6, too.

You can tell from the traceplot that it's not purely an adaptation
problem.

- Bob

On Tuesday, March 11, 2014 8:11:54 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Should we create a separate repo for problematic model/data + sampling

I don't know if we need a separate repo, but there is no great shortage of flaky BUGS examples. All of these were for 21 chains with a base seed of 12345 that is advanced by the chain_id but otherwise kept the default settings

Stan doesn't parse: fire
Stan blows up: salm2, salm, orange
Stan takes way too long: schools (not eight_schools)
Stan doesn't converge: hepatitisME, hepatitis, air, eyes
Stan has bad mixing at a minimum: blocker, kidney, leukfr, magnesium, seeds, birats, stagnant

In each of these cases (except fire), the model wasn't much better with JAGS, so I think it is more a situation where the models are bad (gamma(0,0) priors, etc.). And it underscores that these BUGS examples are not good for unit-testing, but it would be nice if Stan could do a little better.

Ben

That's what I was saying that we need to try it out by default, particularly on Windows, for a little while before merging Michael's branch.

Yes, it says so on that page "R-patched subsequent to Jan 22, 2012, R-devel, and releases after 2.14.1 will use a new toolchain based on pre-4.6.3 gcc, put together by Prof. Brian Ripley" but more useful is

http://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_flavors.html

> It'd be nice if they said which tools were included :-)  And why in
> the world don't they freeze a version for the latest release of R?

They bridge Rtools releases over R releases, so the currently unfrozen version of Rtools will work for R 3.1 when it is released in April and then Rtools will be frozen sometime thereafter. And a new unfrozen version will be started that works with 3.1 and 3.2. That said, they haven't actually changed much in Rtools for a couple of years.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: example of flaky chain
messages.body_plain:
There weren't any recent prior discussions.

To bring you up to speed, we've been planning to set up a repo
that has models that don't work, an explanation of why, a fixed version,
and an explanation of the fix.

Ben's listing some of the BUGS models that don't work in
Stan (or apparently very well in BUGS, either).  The issue
is priors.

We also want to make a practice of storing this kind of
before and after remodeling (that was my best pun in ages) for
user-submitted models.

- Bob

> Bob: please include me to the prior discussions.
>
> Aki
>
> tiistai, 11. maaliskuuta 2014 15.32.46 UTC+2 Bob Carpenter kirjoitti:
>> So the question is whether we should "fix" the priors in those
>>
>> models to be more reasonable.  I'll ping Andrew separately, as he
>>
>> seems to be ignoring stan-dev, and will have the strongest opinions
>>
>> on these.
>>
>>
>>
>> We want examples people can follow to build models.  Comparisons with
>>
>> JAGS isn't the major goal any more, I don't think.
>>
>>
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>> On Mar 11, 2014, at 2:16 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>
>>
>>> On Tuesday, March 11, 2014 8:11:54 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>>> Should we create a separate repo for problematic model/data + sampling
>>
>>> configs?
>>
>>>
>>
>>> I don't know if we need a separate repo, but there is no great shortage of flaky BUGS examples. All of these were for 21 chains with a base seed of 12345 that is advanced by the chain_id but otherwise kept the default settings
>>
>>>
>>
>>> Stan doesn't parse: fire
>>
>>> Stan blows up: salm2, salm, orange
>>
>>> Stan takes way too long: schools (not eight_schools)
>>
>>> Stan doesn't converge: hepatitisME, hepatitis, air, eyes
>>
>>> Stan has bad mixing at a minimum: blocker, kidney, leukfr, magnesium, seeds, birats, stagnant
>>
>>>
>>
>>> In each of these cases (except fire), the model wasn't much better with JAGS, so I think it is more a situation where the models are bad (gamma(0,0) priors, etc.). And it underscores that these BUGS examples are not good for unit-testing, but it would be nice if Stan could do a little better.
>>
>>>
>>
>>> Ben

messages.body_plain:
Ben is the man. After about half an hour of looking at incomprehensible error messages, he asked "how old is your hard drive?" I told him that I didn't know and then he said he thought my disk was corrupt. He had to leave to teach class.

I rebooted the Mac, ran the disk utility, and found that my disk was corrupt. I spent a few minutes repairing the disk and now it runs.

Ben, I owe you. Next round of drinks are on me.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:

1) if I run make check and it runs successfully or fails while running the vignette examples, it will remove ~/.R/Makevars from my machine.

2) I didn't realized I was running off my refactor branch. The develop branch runs fine with parallel, so it must be something in the changed code. I'll try to get that fixed.

Daniel

Ben

messages.subject: Callbacks in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
I'll start with the use-case. In RStan, there's a function called 'run_markov_chain()' that mirrors Stan's function. I'd post the code, but it's not really useful as is. The substantive difference between the two functions is that RStan has one additional line:

    R_CheckUserInterrupt();

RStan calls that function to check whether or not the user has interrupted the process within a for loop. (For the time being, I'm going to ignore the danger in leaving dangling resources. This is how RStan currently works now and I'm just trying to refactor the code so we share more common code.)

My question is, should I just add a function pointer to the method to deal with this interrupt handler? Is there a different pattern we should adopt to make it cleaner?

Is this going to introduce too much overhead? What's the cleanest way to deal with an empty function? CmdStan doesn't need this call, so what should we do about it? Do I create two functions in Stan to maintain efficiency at the cost of duplicating code (one with and without this argument)?

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
I see. I still think that logic can be pushed into Stan.

Let's get down to the implementation level, then. Here's RStan's function:
    template <class Model, class RNG_t>
    void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler_ptr,
                          const stan_args& args,
                          bool is_warmup,
                          mcmc_output<Model>& outputter,
                          stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
                          Model& model,
                          std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& chains,
                          int& iter_save_i,
                          const std::vector<size_t>& qoi_idx,
                          std::vector<double>& sum_pars,
                          double& sum_lp,
                          std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& sampler_params,
                          std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& iter_params,
                          std::string& adaptation_info,
                          RNG_t& base_rng) {
      int start = 0;
      int end = args.get_ctrl_sampling_warmup();
      if (!is_warmup) {
        start = end;
        end = args.get_iter();
      }
      for (int m = start; m < end; ++m) {
        stan::common::print_progress(m, 0, args.get_iter(),
                                     args.get_ctrl_sampling_refresh(), is_warmup,
                                     "\r", "", rstan::io::rcout);
        R_CheckUserInterrupt();
        init_s = sampler_ptr -> transition(init_s);
        if (args.get_ctrl_sampling_save_warmup() && (((m - start) % args.get_ctrl_sampling_thin()) == 0)) {
          outputter.output_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, sampler_ptr, model,
                                        chains, is_warmup,
                                        sampler_params, iter_params,
                                        sum_pars, sum_lp, qoi_idx,
                                        iter_save_i, &rstan::io::rcout);
          iter_save_i++;
          outputter.output_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler_ptr);
        }
      }
    }

Here's Stan's function:
    template <class Model, class RNG>
    void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler,
                          int num_iterations,
                          int start,
                          int finish,
                          int num_thin,
                          int refresh,
                          bool save,
                          bool warmup,
                          stan::io::mcmc_writer<Model>& writer,
                          stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
                          Model& model,
                          RNG& base_rng) {

      for (int m = 0; m < num_iterations; ++m) {

        print_progress(m, start, finish, refresh, warmup);

        init_s = sampler->transition(init_s);

        if ( save && ( (m % num_thin) == 0) ) {
          writer.print_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, *sampler, model);
          writer.print_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler);
        }

      }

    }

I think the sampler->transition() call is the level you're talking about (unless I'm missing something). This is wrapping that call and putting it in a loop and printing where appropriate.

Of course, I might be missing the forest for the trees here. I'm trying to consolidate code in the least error prone manner possible. Here's what I'm thinking should happen with the run_markov_chain function within Stan:

    template <class Model, class RNG>
    void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler,

                          int num_iterations,
                          int start,
                          int finish,
                          int num_thin,
                          int refresh,
                          bool save,
                          bool warmup,
                          stan::io::mcmc_writer<Model>& writer,
                          stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
                          Model& model,

                          RNG& base_rng,
                          std::string &prefix,  // rstan would use "\r", stan uses ""
                          std::ostream& ostream, // rstan uses rstan::io::rcout, stan uses std::cout
                          void (*interrupt_handler)(void)) {  // rstan uses R_CheckUserInterrupt(), stan uses nothing.

      for (int m = 0; m < num_iterations; ++m) {

        print_progress(m, start, finish, refresh, warmup,
                               prefix, ostream);

        interrupt_handler();   // <<<<----- here's the interrupt handler and the real change to behavior

        init_s = sampler->transition(init_s);

        if ( save && ( (m % num_thin) == 0) ) {
          writer.print_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, *sampler, model);
          writer.print_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler);
        }

      }

    }

And the only thing I would really have to do is make sure the writer interface is abstract enough for RStan to implement and provide.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Callbacks in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
I'd much rather see the callback passed in as a functor
rather than as a C-style function pointer.

So that'd add a template parameter

   template <class Model, class RNG, class CB>
   ...
       const CB& c) {
     ...
     c();
   }

and then just call the argument as a functor.  We'd have
to supply a dummy functor for CmdStan.  If you do go with the pointer,
you may just want to check if it's zero and maybe have it
default to 0.

In fact, we should be making the template functionals
for autodiff we're using now constant references instead
of copying them.

Back on topic, here's an example:

#include <iostream>

struct fun {
  fun() { }
  void operator()() const {
    std::cout << "hello" << std::endl;
  }
};

template <typename F>
void foo(const F& f) {
  f();
}

int main() {
  fun callback;
  foo(callback);
}

- Bob

On Mar 12, 2014, at 7:14 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> Of course, I might be missing the forest for the trees here. I'm trying to consolidate code in the least error prone manner possible. Here's what I'm thinking should happen with the run_markov_chain function within Stan:
>
>     template <class Model, class RNG>
>     void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler,
>                           int num_iterations,
>                           int start,
>                           int finish,
>                           int num_thin,
>                           int refresh,
>                           bool save,
>                           bool warmup,
>                           stan::io::mcmc_writer<Model>& writer,
>                           stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
>                           Model& model,
>                           RNG& base_rng,
>                           std::string &prefix,  // rstan would use "\r", stan uses ""
>                           std::ostream& ostream, // rstan uses rstan::io::rcout, stan uses std::cout
>                           void (*interrupt_handler)(void)) {  // rstan uses R_CheckUserInterrupt(), stan uses nothing.
>
>       for (int m = 0; m < num_iterations; ++m) {
>
>         print_progress(m, start, finish, refresh, warmup,
>                                prefix, ostream);
>
>         interrupt_handler();   // <<<<----- here's the interrupt handler and the real change to behavior
>
>         init_s = sampler->transition(init_s);
>
>         if ( save && ( (m % num_thin) == 0) ) {
>           writer.print_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, *sampler, model);
>           writer.print_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler);
>         }
>
>       }
>
>     }
>
>
> And the only thing I would really have to do is make sure the writer interface is abstract enough for RStan to implement and provide.
>
>
>
> On Wed, Mar 12, 2014 at 1:38 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> I see. I still think that logic can be pushed into Stan.
>
> Let's get down to the implementation level, then. Here's RStan's function:
>     template <class Model, class RNG_t>
>     void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler_ptr,
>                           const stan_args& args,
>                           bool is_warmup,
>                           mcmc_output<Model>& outputter,
>                           stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
>                           Model& model,
>                           std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& chains,
>                           int& iter_save_i,
>                           const std::vector<size_t>& qoi_idx,
>                           std::vector<double>& sum_pars,
>                           double& sum_lp,
>                           std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& sampler_params,
>                           std::vector<Rcpp::NumericVector>& iter_params,
>                           std::string& adaptation_info,
>                           RNG_t& base_rng) {
>       int start = 0;
>       int end = args.get_ctrl_sampling_warmup();
>       if (!is_warmup) {
>         start = end;
>         end = args.get_iter();
>       }
>       for (int m = start; m < end; ++m) {
>         stan::common::print_progress(m, 0, args.get_iter(),
>                                      args.get_ctrl_sampling_refresh(), is_warmup,
>                                      "\r", "", rstan::io::rcout);
>         R_CheckUserInterrupt();
>         init_s = sampler_ptr -> transition(init_s);
>         if (args.get_ctrl_sampling_save_warmup() && (((m - start) % args.get_ctrl_sampling_thin()) == 0)) {
>           outputter.output_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, sampler_ptr, model,
>                                         chains, is_warmup,
>                                         sampler_params, iter_params,
>                                         sum_pars, sum_lp, qoi_idx,
>                                         iter_save_i, &rstan::io::rcout);
>           iter_save_i++;
>           outputter.output_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler_ptr);
>         }
>       }
>     }
>
>
> Here's Stan's function:
>     template <class Model, class RNG>
>     void run_markov_chain(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler,
>                           int num_iterations,
>                           int start,
>                           int finish,
>                           int num_thin,
>                           int refresh,
>                           bool save,
>                           bool warmup,
>                           stan::io::mcmc_writer<Model>& writer,
>                           stan::mcmc::sample& init_s,
>                           Model& model,
>                           RNG& base_rng) {
>
>       for (int m = 0; m < num_iterations; ++m) {
>
>         print_progress(m, start, finish, refresh, warmup);
>
>         init_s = sampler->transition(init_s);
>
>         if ( save && ( (m % num_thin) == 0) ) {
>           writer.print_sample_params(base_rng, init_s, *sampler, model);
>           writer.print_diagnostic_params(init_s, sampler);
>         }
>
>       }
>
>     }
>
>
> I think the sampler->transition() call is the level you're talking about (unless I'm missing something). This is wrapping that call and putting it in a loop and printing where appropriate.
>
>
>
>
> On Wed, Mar 12, 2014 at 1:31 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> While I don't think a per-iteration null callback function
> is going to be noticeable speed-wise, I prefer Michael's suggestion
> to set up the interface so that clients pull iterations rather
> than inject callbacks.
>
> That is, assuming I'm interpreting it right.  Rather than
> generate_warmup_transition(), I'd call it something like
> get_next_warmup() or get_warmup().
>
> - Bob
>
> On Mar 12, 2014, at 6:23 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > It should be easy enough to provide API functions for
> >
> > initialize
> > generate_warmup_transition()
> > generate_sample_transition()
> >
> > as well as
> >
> > warmup {
> >   for(n in n_samples)
> >    generate_warmup_transition();
> > }
> >
> > and then just have the interfaces ignore the warmup function
> > if it has to get inside?  At least then the code duplication is
> > minimal.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Wed, Mar 12, 2014 at 5:19 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> > I'll start with the use-case. In RStan, there's a function called 'run_markov_chain()' that mirrors Stan's function. I'd post the code, but it's not really useful as is. The substantive difference between the two functions is that RStan has one additional line:
> >
> >     R_CheckUserInterrupt();
> >
> > RStan calls that function to check whether or not the user has interrupted the process within a for loop. (For the time being, I'm going to ignore the danger in leaving dangling resources. This is how RStan currently works now and I'm just trying to refactor the code so we share more common code.)
> >

> >

> >
> >
> > Daniel

messages.body_plain:
I just realized that if you implement it the way I suggested,
you can also pass in functions!

#include <iostream>

struct fun {
  fun() { }
  void operator()() const {
    std::cout << "hello" << std::endl;
  }
};

template <typename F>
void foo(const F& f) {
  f();
}

void bar() {
  std::cout << "bar" << std::endl;

}

int main() {
  fun callback;
  foo(callback);

  foo(bar);
}

This compiles and prints:

hello
bar

Here's a nice little tutorial:

  http://www.cprogramming.com/tutorial/functors-function-objects-in-c++.html

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, March 12, 2014 4:18:41 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Can you give me a spec of what you need? and what it'll look like exactly?

This is probably at least 99% correct

make --dry-run src/test/unit src/test/unit-agrad-rev src/test/unit-agrad-fwd | grep -o "^test.* " > tests.txt

We need a text file with one autonomous test per line. Basically, you end of passing a sequence of line numbers to the cluster, and it extracts the corresponding like from tests.txt and calls

make ${LINE}

> Or what you're doing now and I'll duplicate. I'll get on that machine and try it out.

After you log into yetisubmit.cc.columbia.edu <http://yetisubmit.cc.columbia.edu> do

cd /vega/stats/projects/stan

and in the yeti subdirectory of that there are two bash files run_refactor_Jenkins.sh (which is the driver) and test.sh (which is called on each line in tests.txt). We just need to clean those up and do something similar for CmdStan. Then, we need some way of linking it with the Windows Jenkins box and be able to trigger it automatically or manually.

Ben

messages.subject: Defining Priors on Latent Spaces
messages.body_plain:
Although our data types allow us to transform from constrained space to unconstrained spaces under the hood, this mapping isn't really exposed to the users.  This limits well-defined priors to those that we have coded by hand, for example

simplex ~ Dirichlet
cov_matrix ~ LKJ

and prohibits non-parametric approaches like assigning a (n - 1)-dimensional GP to the latent space of the simplex.  Should we expose some more functionality here?  I'm thinking either exposing functions

simplex_transform : R^{n - 1} -> R^{n}
simplex_jacobian: R^{n - 1} -> R

so that the user can model the (n - 1)-dimensional space directly and then map to the observation space in transformed parameters in order to define the likelihood, or providing a generic function

simplex_distribution: (n - 1)-dimensional distribution -> n-dimensional distribution

where we take care of any Jacobian business, if necessary.

Thoughts?

messages.subject: variable declarations in functions: spec revision
messages.subject_clean: variable declarations in functions: spec revision
messages.body_plain:
As I'm starting to code the function parser, two things struck
me that I'm going to propose to re-specify.

1.  If we require sizes for functions, we won't actually have a function
definition language that's strong enough to define the Stan built-in
functions!

For instance, we can't define a function with signature

   real sum(vector v);

because we'd need to declare it with a size, as in this minimal signature:

  real sum(int K, vector[K] v);

and then it'll have to be called with something like
sum(K,v) if K is the size of v, or sum(size(v),v).  Either
way, it seems really clunky.

2.  If we have constraints for functions, their signatures won't look
anything like the signatures we have for built-in functions, which are
not specified with constraints.

I'm also worried that if we let users define functions with constrained
type arguments, they may think they need to pass in an argument of that type.

REVISED PROPOSAL
----------------

I propose to allow functions to be declared as in the manual function
signatures, as in:

  real sum(vector x) {
    real sum_x;
    sum_x <- 0;
    for (k in 1:size(x))
      sum_x <- sum_x + x[k];
    return sum_x;
  }

Users can write their own constraints.  If they call
call functions with constraints, the constraints will propagate.

For arrays, I propose to follow the syntax I introduced in
the manual for standalone basic type definitions.  For example, to
sum a 2D array:

  real sum(real[,] x);

Return types use the same syntax.  For example, to create a 2D array:

  real[,] fill_2d_array(real val, int M, int N);

This may be confusing for matrices, where

  matrix[,] foo();

declares the return type to be a 2D array of matrices.
Users might think this is just a matrix return because of
the two indices.

ALTERNATIVE

We could instead require the brackets for the vector/matrix indices
to be given explicitly, as in

  real sum(vector[] x);

where those brackets are just for the vector's index.  Then we could
use:

  real sum(vector[][,] x);

for something that summed a two-dimensional array of vectors.   This
doesn't match what I've done in the manual and is also just plain clunky.

I like the first proposal better than the alternative.

- Bob

messages.subject: Model Consultation Procedure
messages.body_plain:
Stan Users:

With a rapidly expanding community, and an even faster growing list of features
to implement, helping users to understand and optimize their models is becoming
a bit overwhelming.  Of course we don’t want to limit the help we can provide and
so in an effort to reduce redundant answers and provide more resources to users
new to Stan we are hoping to formalize our consultation procedure.

Firstly, when asking a question please try to provide as much information as possible
and be specific with your issues.

Providing a model with an init file and (pseudo)data, especially a simplified model that
manifests the pathology you are seeing, is the best way to provide context to your
question.  Also please be aware that not everyone uses the same interfaces, and
so providing your model in as many formats as possible will significantly improve
the probability of a prompt response (currently many devs use CmdStan, and Rstan
provides various functions for outputting data frames into compatible formats).
Also, please follow the style guidelines in the manual!  The easier it is for
someone to read your model the faster we’ll be able to respond.

Specificity is also critical.  Complaining of a “slow” model is extremely ambiguous,
whereas small ESS, large Rhat, and reduced ESS/time are much more informative
and allow us to identify possible issues immediately.

Secondly, we would like go curate many of these questions into reference models
and provide new users a suite of illustrative examples in model building, validation,
and optimization.  Each entry will include a user summary of the problem and its
resolution, developer notes adding supporting information and references, and
(possibly simplified) models a user can run themselves.

If you are interested in participating then please indicate as much as the beginning
of your question along with the open source license under which you would prefer the
discussion and any subsequent models to be released.

Thanks!

The Stan Development Team

messages.subject: Jenkins pull request admin privileges
messages.body_plain:
When we first went to a gitflow-like process, I added Bob and myself as admins. It was only meant to be a limited group until we kind of got the process down and understood the bottleneck and how it affected our build server.

I just added the whole stan-dev member list to the white list, so any pull request created by us will kick off a build. Any additional commits on existing pull requests will also create more test jobs. I added the organization, so hopefully any future changes will reflect on that list.

I added, by hand, all the existing members to the admin list on Jenkins. The commands to control Jenkins:
- "Jenkins, ok to test" -- accept to testing phase for a pull request by a member not on the white list. This should kick off a build automatically.
- "Jenkins, test this please" or "Jenkins, retest this please" -- will put a build on the testing queue.

Marcus, can you try the test phrase on the last pull request again? I didn't get around to updating Jenkins until just now.

Just a reminder, this is where Jenkins is located on the web:
http://d1m1s1b1.stat.columbia.edu:8080/

Daniel

messages.subject: Metropolis Hastings in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Sebastian.   We discussed this at the Stan meeting and the sense is that this is doable, that the best way to do this will be for the user to supply a covariance matrix for the Metropolis jumping kernel (with an identity matrix as the default) and then Stan-Metropolis would autotune the scale of the matrix to a 0.234 acceptance rate.  It would be too much of an effort to auto-tune the entire covariance matrix (because of the possibility of introducing instability) but it should be no problem to adapt a single scalar multiplier.  The user could then do more tuning as desired by simply calling Stan-Metropolis more than once (e.g., running it a the default cov matrix, then using the simulations thus far as a scaling matrix for the next step).  According to Bob, we pretty much already have Metrop implemented within Stan, so if someone wants to implement the scalar auto-tuning and do all the testing, I guess it would be good to go.
A

My understanding is that it just wouldn't converge for
the BUGS models.  Has anyone ever done this kind of large-scale
random-walk Metropolis test and figured out a good way to
adapt the jumping covariance?

I think I see where Andrew was going with Metropolis-adjusted
Langevin (aka MALA) --- if we do just configure Stan to do
1-step HMC, then the effect is

  * randomly generate a normal(0,1) momentum

  * take 1 leapfrog step in direction of momentum over mass
    (step size = time)

That's like taking a normal(0,Sigma) random walk step if step size = 1,
right?

Then we could use Stan to adapt step size to a fixed target
acceptance probability (already implemented), and to estimate
a diagonal or dense mass matrix (or we could set to diagonal).
That's all implemented.

What we still need to do is implement inputs for a diagonal or
full mass matrix, and then you can basically specify a random-walk
Metropolis with normal jumps with a given covariance matrix.

- Bob

It would be too much of an effort to auto-tune the entire covariance matrix (because of the possibility of introducing instability) but it should be no problem to adapt a single scalar multiplier.  The user could then do more tuning as desired by simply calling Stan-Metropolis more than once (e.g., running it a the default cov matrix, then using the simulations thus far as a scaling matrix for the next step). Some of the BUGS models don't converge with NUTS or Gibbs sampling either, but most do. MCMCpack has random-walk Metropolis that by default uses the MLEs plus a diagonal matrix of scaling parameters to jump.

I don't recall anyone on stan-users wanting to compare Metropolis-Hastings to NUTS, usually it is BUGS to NUTS. I did a few comparisons for my class, and you get pictures like this:

Hi,

I've noticed a new genre in blog posts about software, e.g.,

- This Week in Rust (Mozilla's new systems programming language) (http://cmr.github.io/blog/2014/02/09/this-week-in-rust/)
- This Week in Cyanogenmod (http://www.cyanogenmod.org/blog/this-week-in-cm-mar-21-2014)

a feed reader at it. I imagine some people might prefer that to following
activity on the mailing list.

Best wishes,

-a
